title: The stroke read-back
goal: Know what `resolve` and `lookup` print for a stroke that is not in the dictionary, and the rules that reading follows.

blocks.x: What it is

`Rules::resolve` takes a stroke (or `+`-joined run) that missed the dictionary and reads its keys back into sounds, using the same onset, vowel and coda tables the generator writes with, in reverse. It spells the sounds plainly, because no word is on record to give a real spelling. Every key means something on its own and the vowel table covers all 15 non-empty vowel-key combinations, so almost every stroke reads back as something.

No engine runs this reading: a live steno engine types a stroke that misses the dictionary as its raw keys, and lyk ships no plugin to change that. The reading is what `resolve` and `lookup` print for a miss, and what the site's trainer shows. Treat it as a way to check that a stroke you improvised is a sensible one.
The rules of the read-back
A vowelless stroke reads with no invented vowel
`-T` alone reads `t`, with no guessed vowel. A stroke with consonants and no vowel key is a bare continuation, valid as it is.
A suffix stroke always reads as that suffix

For any stroke after the first that carries the join key, `!resolve` first checks `rules/suffixes.toml`'s chords, before the ordinary read-back. So `+-D` after a stroke with no entry reads `!ed`, not the bare consonant `d`.

items: A two-stroke suffix is checked first, as a pair: `-ism` `+EUZ/+-PL`, `-ity` `+U/+TEU`.
This is unconditional: a suffix does not need a particular composed outline to be a dictionary entry already.
A suffix struck alone, with no stroke before it, is already a literal dictionary entry; `!resolve` is never reached for it.

blocks.x: See the [suffix table](#/ref/suffixes).
A placed single-stroke word as the stem reads as its own text

When the run's first stroke is already a single-stroke word, `!resolve` uses that word's real text instead of decoding the keys. [[and|SKP]] is a brief with no phonetic link to its spelling, so `SKP/+-R` reads `!ander`, not `sper`. Rules-derived words get the same treatment: [[build|PWHR]] plus `+-D` reads `builded`.

items: Only the first stroke of a run longer than one stroke. A single stroke that matches a placed word is a normal dictionary hit.
Only a single-stroke stem. A multi-stroke placed word as the stem of an unmatched run is not covered yet.

blocks.x: Silent e before a vowel ending
English spelling is not plain concatenation, so `!resolve` looks at the first letter of the next piece before it commits the stem:

blocks.x: Not covered: `dye` and `singe` keep their `e` before `-ing` to stay distinct from `die` and `sing`.
A true miss
The only stroke the rules give up on is one with nothing left once the star and join keys are set aside: no onset, no vowel, no coda. A star and a join key alone carry no sound.
Vowel keys and ties

items: Every vowel-key combination is a different vowel: `AO` and `AOU` read differently, so `-T/+AO` and `-T/+AOU` are different words.

Two sounds can share the same keys (`Z` and the silent-glide cluster `Z Y` are both `STKPW`; a plain vowel and a spelling variant can be the same keys). The read-back resolves such a tie **the same way every time**, so a given miss always reads the same. It is consistent, not necessarily what you meant.

blocks.x: Bare `AO` is a three-way tie: `UH` (*book*, *put*), `UW.oo` (*too*, *moon*, *kangaroo*) and `OW.oa` (*boat*). A word's full pronunciation settles this when the dictionary is built; a miss has no word, so `!resolve` picks **`UW.oo`**, because `UH` is rare as an unreduced vowel on a continuation stroke, where "-oo" endings are common. The tie-break is `vowel_rank` in `src/rules/mod.rs`.
Try it

cargo run --release -- resolve STKPW         # a stroke not in the dictionary, read back
cargo run --release -- resolve -- "-T/+-D"     # a run, read back
cargo run --release -- resolve -- "-T/+AOU"    # a continuation with the AOU vowel

`!resolve` (alias `stroke`) prints what the outline types in quotes, with a note when the dictionary has no entry and the quoted word is the rules' reading of it, then the entries nearest to it (see [the interactive session](#/ref/build-and-files/the-interactive-session)). Many `+`-joined runs are already backup entries, so the read-back only matters for runs the dictionary lacks.
